what_its_for: Bortezomib is a cancer medicine used to treat multiple myeloma (a type of blood cancer) and mantle cell lymphoma (a type of lymph node cancer). It works by blocking certain proteins inside cancer cells, which causes the cancer cells to die.
how_to_take: Bortezomib is given as an injection — either as a shot under the skin (subcutaneous) or directly into a vein (intravenous). A healthcare provider, nurse, or doctor will always give you this injection at a clinic or hospital. You will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home. Each treatment session is quick, usually just a few seconds to a few minutes.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the exact dose based on your body size, the type of cancer you have, and your overall health. Treatments are usually given on specific days of a cycle — for example, twice a week for 2 weeks, followed by a 10-day rest period. Your treatment schedule will be carefully planned and explained by your cancer care team. Never change your schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given at a clinic by a healthcare provider, missing a dose is less likely, but it can happen if you miss an appointment. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team as soon as possible. Do not try to 'make up' a missed dose on your own — your doctor will decide the best time to give the next dose safely.
storage: Your healthcare provider or pharmacy will store and handle this medicine for you. The medicine comes as a powder that must be mixed before use and is stored refrigerated or at room temperature depending on how it is prepared. You do not need to store it at home.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking grapefruit juice or eating grapefruit, as it may affect how this medicine works. Avoid taking new medications — including vitamins, supplements, and herbal products like St. John's Wort — without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist, as many drugs can interact with bortezomib. Avoid people who are sick or have infections, since this medicine can lower your ability to fight germs. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, faint, or have blurry vision, as bortezomib can sometimes affect your balance and eyesight.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: numbness, tingling, burning, or pain in your hands or feet (nerve pain); severe dizziness or fainting; chest pain or shortness of breath; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or cough; unusual bruising or bleeding; severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; swelling of the face, lips, or throat; vision changes; extreme tiredness or weakness; or dark urine or yellowing of the skin or eyes.
when_it_works: It may take several weeks to months before you notice improvements. Your doctor will check your blood tests and do regular exams to see how well the treatment is working. Every person responds differently, so be patient and keep all of your scheduled appointments.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially nerve problems and low blood pressure — tell your doctor if you feel dizzy when standing up. If you have liver problems, your dose may need to be adjusted. This medicine should NOT be used during pregnancy, as it can harm an unborn baby. Both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and for several months after the last dose. If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before starting this medicine, as it is not known if it passes into breast milk. Children: safety and dosing in children have not been fully established.
